docs.title: CoreTech: Why Keyboards Matter
docs.text:
Course package

Outcome level: 1 - Has Knowledge Competencies: Keyboards Content type: content 4 lessons · about 4.0 hours Built from: main

You are reading the reviewer view -- the complete package, including the design document, mentor guide and the quiz answer key.

A short course on why default keyboards fall short for language technology work, and how Keyman solves the problem. Developed and drafted in Cypher for Business, but not yet delivered to learners there or anywhere else; this repo's content was revised from a Claude.ai-chat draft with every specific technical claim verified live against Windows 11 + Keyman by the SME — see 00-design.md for the full verification record.

docs.text:
• Module 1: Why Virtual Keyboards Matter
  • Module 2: Installing Keyman and Keyboards
  • Module 3: Configuring System Settings
  • Module 4: Troubleshooting Common Issues
  • Quizzes: Module 1 Check-in & Final Assessment

The PDF quick guide referenced in the Cypher draft is saved to this folder as Quick_Guide_Keyman_Windows_A5_With_Cover.pdf. The original Cypher HTML exports (Cypher-module_N.html) and QTI quiz exports (qti_va_*.zip) are kept for provenance — they're the draft this revision started from, not the current source of truth. The "Revision with chipp.ai" section (an interactive AI tutor tool, not static lesson content) was never in scope for backfill.

Deployment note: the Cypher-module_N.html files reference four decorative section-divider icons (connect.png, content.png, challenge.png, change.png) at Cypher-internal paths. These are dropped from this repo's markdown (replaced with plain bold section labels) since they're presentation, not content — but the same icon filenames and file path appear across other courses too (e.g. coretech-os-basics), suggesting they're a standard, reusable Connect/Content/Challenge/Change icon set already built into Cypher's page template for this curriculum. Whoever re-inserts this course's content back into Cypher should apply that same standard icon set there, rather than treating it as missing content to recreate.

docs.title: SME knowledge notes
docs.text:
Source: four Claude.ai-chat-drafted modules (Module_1_Why_Virtual_Keyboards_Matter.md, Module_2_Installing_Keyman_and_Keyboards.md, Module_3_Configuring_System_Settings.md, Module_4_Troubleshooting_Common_Issues.md), supplied by the SME. The SME reports these were "verified as we went" during the original chat session, but specific claims are being independently re-checked here against live Windows 11 + Keyman, since AI-drafted procedural claims have already proven unreliable once in this repo (FLEx's writing-systems tab, sense-disambiguation right-click).

Confirmed against live Windows 11 + Keyman by the SME: - Shift + Alt + K opens the on-screen keyboard pane — confirmed. This is a Keyman-configurable hotkey (Keyman Configuration → Hotkeys → "Show On Screen Keyboard Pane"), not a generic Windows shortcut — the draft's framing of it as a plain keyboard shortcut should be corrected to reflect that it's a Keyman hotkey setting. - Win + Space cycles installed keyboards — confirmed. - Alt + Shift (specifically Left Alt+Shift, per the Keyman Hotkeys screenshot, where it's bound by default to Keyman's own "Open Language Switcher") does cycle through installed keyboards on Windows 11 — confirmed, but with a real caveat the draft got wrong: it always applies on Screen 1, even if the active program/window is on Screen 2 (a multi-monitor bug). The draft's vague framing ("inconsistent across applications and Windows versions") should be replaced with this specific, accurate behavior. - The Windows Settings path for adding a language is Time & Language → Language & Region → Add a language — the draft said Time & Language → Language (missing "& Region"). Correct this exact path before it goes into lesson content. - The Keyman Configuration → Hotkeys panel (see screenshot on file) shows several configurable hotkeys beyond what the draft mentions: "Open Language Switcher" (default: Left Alt+Shift), "Show On Screen Keyboard Pane" (default: Shift+Alt+K), "Show Font Helper Pane," "Show Character Map," "Open Text Editor" (default: Ctrl+K), "Open Configuration" — most default to "(no hotkey)." A per-keyboard-layout "Change Hotkey" dialog offers No Hotkey / Left Alt+Shift / Ctrl+Shift / Custom (type your own combination). This is richer and more accurate than the draft's brief "look for a Hotkey option" description.

Second round of confirmations (SME, live check + memory): - Language count is wrong in the draft — correct to "more than 2,500 languages." Confirmed via the keyman.com badge graphic ("More than 2500 languages supported"), not the draft's "over 2,000." - keyman.com is now a multilingual site with locale-prefixed URLs. The draft's bare keyman.com/windows should be https://keyman.com/en/windows/ (confirmed via the site's language switcher, which lists English/Deutsch/Español/Français/ Khmer). Apply the same /en/ pattern to keyman.com/keyboards and keyman.com/support unless separately confirmed otherwise. - community.software.sil.org → confirmed, resolves to the "Language Software Community" site; the Keyman-specific area requires scrolling down the page, it's not immediately visible at the top — worth a note in the lesson so learners don't think the link is wrong. - keyman.com/support → confirmed, goes to Keyman Support. - scripts.sil.org → confirmed reachable, but it's an archive of the original site, not an actively-maintained current resource — the lesson should frame it as an archive, not a live go-to support page. - Windows UAC "install permission prompt, even if you're an administrator" (Module 2) — confirmed from memory (not a fresh live re-test), lower confidence than the screenshot-verified items above but accepted. - The video referenced in the Module 1 draft ("Why Keyboarding Matters in Language Work") is the same asset as the real Cypher course's why.mp4 — just referenced by title in the draft rather than filename. The full transcript already captured in the faithfully-backfilled 01-module-1.md is valid and should carry over into the revised Module 1. - Expanded duration (Module 2 ~90 min, Modules 3-4 ~60 min each, vs. the original course's ~20-30 min/module pace) — confirmed intentional, with the caveat that self-paced learners may move faster than the stated estimate.

All items from the design doc's original open-question list are now resolved. Next step: rewrite 01-module-1.md through 04-module-4.md using the Claude-chat drafts as the base, applying every correction above, and reconcile 05-quiz.md against the revised content once that's done.

docs.title: Module 1: Why Virtual Keyboards Matter
docs.text:
Estimated time: 30 minutes

Purpose: Before you can help anyone install or configure a keyboard, you need to understand what problem you're actually solving — and why it's worth taking seriously.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text: By the end of this module, you will be able to: - Explain why default keyboards are insufficient for language technology work - Describe what a virtual keyboard is and how it differs from a physical keyboard layout - Identify Keyman as the standard keyboard solution used in language technology work - Articulate to others why keyboard setup matters for translation, literacy, and publishing

docs.title: Connect
docs.text:
Let's start with something you may have already seen.

Imagine you're helping a community that writes in a script your computer doesn't know about — maybe an African language with special tone marks, or a South or Southeast Asian script. Someone sits down to type, and... nothing works right. The letters come out wrong, or as strange symbols, or nothing comes out at all.

Have you seen something like this? Or maybe you've tried to type in a language yourself and had the same problem.

▶️ Watch: "Why Keyboarding Matters in Language Work" (2 minutes)

That video shows the problem clearly. The gap between what a language community needs and what a standard keyboard provides is one of the biggest — and most ignored — barriers in language work.

✏️ Before you go further: Have you ever seen a typing or display problem in a local language? Write a sentence or two about it. You don't need to solve it yet — just describe what you saw. We'll come back to this at the end of the module.

docs.title: What is a virtual keyboard?
docs.text:
A virtual keyboard is software. When you press a key, the software changes what appears on screen — instead of the letter on your keyboard, you get the letter the language needs.

That's it. It's a layer between your physical keys and the screen. Keyman is the tool we use, and it supports more than 2,500 languages. It's free, it works on Windows (and other systems), and it's trusted by language communities and consultants around the world.

docs.title: Why does this matter for your work?
docs.text:
As a Language Technology Consultant, you often work with communities whose languages aren't supported by default. Without the right keyboard:

  • Text can come out wrong, even when someone types carefully
  • Symbols and special characters go missing
  • Errors creep into Scripture translations, literacy materials, and data
  • People give up and just use the wrong script — which causes more problems later

Knowing how to set up a virtual keyboard is one of the most practical things you can do to help.

docs.title: A quick note about Keyman
docs.text:
Keyman was developed by SIL Global. It's free, open-source, and actively supported. This isn't a workaround or a temporary fix — it's a proper tool, used by serious language work around the world.

TIP You can find keyboards for hundreds of languages at keyman.com/en/keyboards. It's worth exploring even before you need to install anything.

NOTE — Video transcript

Why does keyboarding matter — transcript Why does keyboarding matter in language work? When the characters don't show up right, it's more than a technical glitch — it's a barrier to communication. Many languages use scripts, diacritics, or symbols that aren't on a standard keyboard. Typing becomes frustrating... or impossible. That's why we use tools like Keyman. Keyman lets us install keyboards tailored to the exact writing system we need. Now every character appears as expected. Workflows are smoother. The language is respected and usable in print or apps. As a Language Technology Consultant, you help others overcome these challenges. Keyboard setup is one small step with big impact. When input works, translation, literacy, and publishing can thrive. Because language matters. And every language deserves the tools to be written, read, and shared.

docs.title: Challenge
docs.text:
Here's a small activity before we move on.

✏️ Go to keyman.com/en/keyboards and search for a language you work with, or one you're curious about. Does it have a keyboard listed? Are there more than one? Write down what you found — even "I couldn't find it" is a useful answer.

This isn't a test. It's just to get you familiar with what's there.

docs.title: Change
docs.text:
✏️ Now, write 2–3 sentences: Why does this matter for the work you're part of? What would change for a community you know if their keyboard problem was solved?

Hold onto your answer. It's your motivation for the next three modules.

docs.title: Module 2: Installing Keyman and Keyboards
docs.text:
Estimated time: 90 minutes

Purpose: Understanding why keyboards matter isn't enough — you need to be able to install Keyman and a keyboard yourself before you can walk anyone else through it.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text: By the end of this module, you will be able to: - Install the Keyman program from the web - Install a keyboard for a language you know, either from within Keyman or from keyman.com - Test a newly installed keyboard in a text editor, confirming it produces the correct characters

docs.title: Connect
docs.text:
Before we explain anything, let's try something.

Open Notepad or any word processor. Now try to type a few words in a language you work with that doesn't use the Latin alphabet — just using your normal keyboard.

▶️ Take 2 minutes and try it now.

What came out? Probably not what you wanted. That's the problem we're about to fix.

By the end of this module, you'll be able to type correctly in at least one language. That's the goal.

docs.title: Step 1: Install Keyman
docs.text:
First, we install the Keyman engine — the software that makes everything work.

  1. Go to keyman.com/en/windows
  2. Click Download Keyman for Windows
  3. Open the file when it finishes downloading
  4. Windows will ask for permission to install — click Yes. This is normal, even if you're an administrator.
  5. Keyman will open automatically. Look for its small icon in the bottom-right corner of your screen (near the clock). That's the system tray.

TIP Can't see the icon? Click the small upward arrow (︿) near the clock. Some icons hide there.

Keyman is now installed, but it doesn't have any keyboards yet. Think of it as an empty container — we need to add keyboards next.

docs.title: Step 2: Install a keyboard
docs.text:
You can find keyboards two ways.

From inside Keyman: 1. Click the Keyman icon in the system tray 2. Open Keyman Configuration 3. Go to Keyboard Layouts and click Download keyboard 4. Search for your language and install

From the website: 1. Go to keyman.com/en/keyboards 2. Search for your language 3. Click Install — this opens Keyman and finishes from there

TIP You might see several keyboards listed for one language. That's normal — different keyboards suit different purposes. If you're not sure which to pick, look for one marked "recommended" or read the short description.

If someone gives you a .kmp file (a Keyman package file), you don't need to search online. Just double-click the file and Keyman will install it for you.

docs.title: Step 3: Test it
docs.text:
Let's make sure it works before we go any further.

  1. Open Notepad
  2. Click the Keyman icon and select your new keyboard from the list
  3. Press Shift + Alt + K to open the on-screen keyboard pane, so you can see what each key will type
  4. Try typing. Compare what appears on screen with the keyboard picture.

NOTE Shift + Alt + K is one of Keyman's built-in configurable hotkeys (Keyman Configuration → Hotkeys → "Show On Screen Keyboard Pane"), not a generic Windows shortcut — you'll see the full Hotkeys panel in Module 3.

TIP Check the system tray icon — it shows which keyboard is active. If you're typing but getting the wrong characters, this is the first place to look.

docs.title: Challenge
docs.text:
Now do it yourself, from the beginning.

✏️ Install Keyman and at least one keyboard for a language you work with. Then open Notepad and type at least one sentence using that keyboard.

✏️ Take a screenshot of your typed text. Make sure the Keyman icon is visible in the system tray. This is your evidence that it's working.

Don't skip ahead. If something goes wrong during the installation, that's actually useful — make a note of what happened and check Module 4. Real problems are good practice.

docs.title: Change
docs.text:
✏️ Reflection: What was the hardest part? Was there any step that surprised you or didn't go as expected? Write a short note about it.

This matters because when you help someone else install their first keyboard, you'll remember what tripped you up. That makes you a much better guide.

docs.title: Module 3: Configuring System Settings
docs.text:
Estimated time: 60 minutes

Purpose: A keyboard that requires constant manual switching tends to get abandoned. This module makes keyboard switching seamless instead of a manual chore, so the tool actually gets used day to day.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text: By the end of this module, you will be able to: - Associate a Keyman keyboard with a Windows system language - Configure Windows so the correct keyboard loads automatically when you switch languages - Switch between keyboards reliably, using more than one method

docs.title: Connect
docs.text:
Here's a scenario that comes up constantly in the field: someone has Keyman installed and a keyboard that works perfectly — but every time they open a new application, they have to manually switch back to their language keyboard. The system keeps defaulting to English. It works, but it's annoying enough that some people stop using it.

Quick check: When you switch the display language in Windows settings, does your keyboard automatically change to match? If you're not sure, try it now and see what happens.

This module is about making Windows and Keyman work together properly — so keyboard switching becomes seamless rather than manual.

docs.title: How Windows and Keyman work together
docs.text:
Windows links keyboards to languages. When you switch from English to French, Windows switches to whatever keyboard is assigned to French. We can make Keyman part of that system — so switching to a language in Windows automatically activates your Keyman keyboard.

Once this is set up, you won't need to manually click the Keyman icon every time. The system handles it.

docs.title: Step 1: Link your keyboard to a Windows language
docs.text:
1. Click the Keyman icon → open Keyman Configuration
  2. Find your keyboard in the list
  3. Look for an option to associate it with a Windows language
  4. Select the matching language (for example, link an Amharic keyboard to Amharic)
  5. Click OK

TIP If the language you need isn't in the Windows list, you'll need to add it first. Go to Windows Settings → Time & Language → Language & Region → Add a language. After that, come back and finish the Keyman step.

docs.title: Step 2: Make Keyman the default keyboard for that language
docs.text:
Adding a language to Windows doesn't automatically use your Keyman keyboard. Windows might assign a different keyboard instead. Here's how to fix that:

  1. Go to Windows Settings → Time & Language → Language & Region
  2. Click on your language → Options
  3. Under Keyboards, you should see your Keyman keyboard. If something else is listed first, remove it, or move Keyman to the top.

After this, Windows will use your Keyman keyboard automatically whenever that language is active.

docs.title: Step 3: Switch between keyboards
docs.text:
There are a few ways to switch between keyboards when you're working.

  • Method 1 — Keyman icon: Click the Keyman icon in the system tray and select the keyboard you want from the list. This always works and is the most reliable method.
  • Method 2 — Windows keyboard shortcut: Press Win + Space to cycle through your installed system languages (including Keyman keyboards).
  • Method 3 — Keyman's Open Language Switcher hotkey: Keyman itself has a configurable "Open Language Switcher" hotkey, bound by default to Left Alt + Shift. It does cycle through your installed keyboards on Windows 11.

WARNING Left Alt + Shift has a real quirk worth knowing about: it always applies on Screen 1 of a multi-monitor setup, even if the window you're actually working in is on Screen 2. If you use two monitors and switching seems to do nothing, check whether it actually switched on the other screen before assuming it's broken.

docs.title: Setting custom hotkeys
docs.text:
Keyman Configuration has its own Hotkeys panel (Keyman Configuration → Hotkeys), separate from Windows' own shortcuts. It lists several configurable actions, most set to "(no hotkey)" by default:

  • Open Language Switcher — default Left Alt + Shift
  • Show On Screen Keyboard Pane — default Shift + Alt + K
  • Show Font Helper Pane
  • Show Character Map
  • Open Text Editor — default Ctrl + K
  • Open Configuration

You can also set a hotkey for an individual keyboard layout. Double-click a keyboard's hotkey field to open the Change Hotkey dialog, which offers No Hotkey, Left Alt + Shift, Ctrl + Shift, or Custom (hold Ctrl/Shift/Alt and type your own combination).

TIP If you switch keyboards frequently and Win + Space or the multi-monitor quirk above is getting in your way, setting a per-keyboard custom hotkey here can save real time — just make sure it doesn't conflict with shortcuts you use in other applications.

docs.title: Challenge
docs.text:
Put this into practice with your installed keyboard.

✏️ Activity 1: Assign your installed keyboard to a Windows language — use Haitian Creole if you want to test with something less likely to conflict with your default setup, or use the language you actually need.

✏️ Activity 2: Switch between your default keyboard and your language keyboard using both the Keyman icon and Win + Space. Confirm that switching works in at least two different applications (e.g., Word and Notepad).

Once you've done both, work through the checklist below and tick each item:

  • Keyboard installed
  • Associated with a Windows system language
  • Keyboard switching works using the Keyman icon
  • Keyboard switching works using Win + Space
  • Switching works in at least two different applications

docs.title: Change
docs.text:
You've now moved from "Keyman is installed" to "Keyman is properly integrated into my system." That's a meaningful step — a keyboard that requires constant manual switching tends to get abandoned.

✏️ Reflection: Think about a colleague or community member you might help set this up for. What's one thing you'd want to make sure they understood before you walked them through this module? Write it down.

Teaching someone else is one of the most powerful ways to consolidate your own learning. If you can explain the why behind each configuration step — not just the how — you're in a strong position to support others.

docs.title: Module 4: Troubleshooting Common Issues
docs.text:
Estimated time: 60 minutes

Purpose: Keyboards that were working can stop working — a Windows update, a new application, an accidental setting change. This module gives you a way to think through problems quickly instead of guessing, so you can help someone else stay calm when it happens to them.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text: By the end of this module, you will be able to: - Sort a keyboard problem into one of four common categories - Apply the matching quick fix for each category - Identify where to find further help when a problem doesn't fit a known pattern

docs.title: Connect
docs.text:
"It worked yesterday — now it's gone."

You've probably heard something like this. Keyboards are reliable when they're set up well, but small things can disrupt them — a Windows update, a new application, clicking the wrong setting by accident.

This module won't make problems disappear. But it will help you think through them quickly, so you can stay calm and figure things out when a community member comes to you frustrated.

docs.title: Start here: what kind of problem is it?
docs.text:
Most keyboard problems are one of four types. Figuring out which one saves a lot of time.

  • Type 1 — The keyboard isn't showing up. The Keyman icon is missing, or the keyboard isn't in the list.
  • Type 2 — The keyboard is active but the wrong characters appear. You selected the right keyboard, but the output is wrong.
  • Type 3 — Switching doesn't work. The keyboard works on its own, but you can't switch to it properly.
  • Type 4 — The characters look wrong. You're typing the right characters, but they appear as boxes or strange symbols.

Each type has a different fix. Let's go through them.

docs.title: Type 1: Keyboard not showing up
docs.text:
If the Keyman icon isn't in the system tray, Keyman might not be running. Search for Keyman in the Start Menu and open it. This should bring it back.

If the icon is there but your keyboard isn't listed, open Keyman Configuration and check Keyboard Layouts. The keyboard might have been removed accidentally, or a Keyman update may have reset things. Just reinstall the keyboard.

docs.title: Type 2: Wrong characters appearing
docs.text:
This almost always means the wrong keyboard is selected. Look at the system tray icon — it shows which keyboard is active. Click it and switch to the correct one.

If you have the right keyboard selected but still get wrong characters, open the on-screen keyboard (Shift + Alt + K — Keyman's "Show On Screen Keyboard Pane" hotkey). Compare what the keys show with what you're actually getting. If they don't match, another keyboard might be overriding Keyman.

TIP Some programs have their own language settings that can override the system. If one specific program is causing trouble, check its language or input settings separately.

docs.title: Type 3: Switching doesn't work
docs.text:
Win + Space only works if Windows has more than one language installed. Go to Windows Settings → Time & Language → Language & Region and check. If only one language is there, add another.

If languages are there but switching still doesn't work, set a custom hotkey in Keyman Configuration's Hotkeys panel (see Module 3). This gives you a direct shortcut that doesn't go through Windows at all.

NOTE If Keyman's own Left Alt + Shift language-switcher hotkey seems to do nothing, remember the multi-monitor quirk from Module 3 — it switches on Screen 1 regardless of which screen you're actually working on. Check the other screen before assuming it's broken.

docs.title: Type 4: Characters look wrong (boxes or strange symbols)
docs.text:
This is usually a font problem, not a keyboard problem. The keyboard is working correctly, but the program is using a font that doesn't include those characters. The fix is to change to a font that supports your language's script.

Noto fonts (from Google Fonts) cover a huge range of scripts and are free. SIL also makes fonts for many minority language scripts — an archive of the original scripts.sil.org resources is available at scripts.sil.org (note: this is an archive, not an actively-maintained current site, so treat it as a reference rather than a live support channel).

TIP In Word, it helps to set the font before you start typing in the new language. Changing the font after the fact sometimes works, but starting with the right font is cleaner.

docs.title: Where to get more help
docs.text:
You don't have to figure everything out alone. These are good places to go:

  • community.software.sil.org — the Language Software Community site; for Keyman specifically, you'll need to scroll down the page to find the relevant area, it isn't at the top
  • keyman.com/en/support — official documentation and support articles
  • Your LangTech Consultant network — colleagues have probably seen the same problem

docs.title: Challenge
docs.text:
Reading about troubleshooting is useful. Working through a real problem is better.

✏️ Scenario: The Keyman icon is visible. Your keyboard is listed. You click it, then try to type in Word — but the wrong characters appear. The on-screen keyboard shows the right keys. What would you check? Write down each step you'd take.

There's no single correct answer. The point is to practice the thinking, not find one specific solution. If you want to go further, try deliberately breaking your setup — switch to the wrong keyboard, or change a font — and then troubleshoot back to working.

docs.title: Change
docs.text:
This is the last module. It's a good moment to look back at where you started.

✏️ Final reflection: Go back to what you wrote in Module 1 — the typing or display problem you described. If you saw that same problem today, what would you do? Be specific.

If you can answer that clearly, you've reached the goal. You can now install, configure, and troubleshoot Keyman for Windows — and help others do the same.

docs.title: Course completion
docs.text:
To finish this course, please submit:

  1. A screenshot of text you typed using your installed keyboard (from Module 2)
  2. Your completed checklist (from Module 3)
  3. Your written response to the final reflection (above)

Well done for working through this. These are real skills that make a real difference to the communities and colleagues you work with.

docs.title: Section 1: Module 1 Check-in Quiz
docs.text:
[Source: qti_va_1784569639.zip, the LMS's "Module 1: Why Keyboarding Matters" quiz icon. Note its content actually ranges across system configuration and troubleshooting topics as well as Module 1's own material — that's how it was delivered, not an artifact of this conversion.]

You need 80% (8/10) to pass.

Question 1 (True/False): Default system keyboards may not support all scripts, diacritics, or symbols needed for every language. - A) True - B) False

Question 2 (True/False): Keyman allows users to install keyboards that are tailored to specific writing systems. - A) True - B) False

Question 3 (True/False): Associating a keyboard with a Windows language can help automatically switch to the correct keyboard layout when you change languages. - A) True - B) False

Question 4 (True/False): If a keyboard is not showing up, it might be because Keyman is not running. - A) True - B) False

Question 5 (True/False): Font problems are never a cause of character display issues when using custom keyboards. - A) True - B) False

Question 6: Which of the following are reasons why default system keyboards may not work well for every language? - A) They support every language out of the box. - B) They may lack scripts or diacritics needed for certain languages. - C) They automatically detect and adjust to any language. - D) They prevent barriers to communication.

Question 7: What is one key feature that Keyman offers for language workers? - A) It only works with standard keyboard layouts. - B) It lets you install keyboards tailored to specific writing systems. - C) It translates documents automatically. - D) It blocks unsupported characters.

Question 8 (Select all that apply): When configuring system settings, which methods can be used to switch between keyboards? - A) Hotkeys - B) Language bar - C) Keyman menu - D) Changing the monitor brightness

Question 9: If characters do not display correctly after installing a custom keyboard, what might be the cause? - A) There is a font problem. - B) The computer is unplugged. - C) Keyman is not supported on Windows. - D) The keyboard needs to be cleaned physically.

Question 10: Which steps are recommended to test a newly installed keyboard using Keyman? - A) Only use the keyboard in a web browser. - B) Test in Notepad or Word using both a physical keyboard and an on-screen keyboard. - C) Restart the computer and uninstall Keyman. - D) Send an email to technical support immediately.

docs.title: How to review this
docs.text:
Read the whole package. Check facts, tool names, menu paths and versions against reality (stage 5), and the teaching, tone and ordering as if you were the learner (stage 6).

Leave feedback as a comment on the course's pull request (line by line on the Files changed tab) or on its tracker issue. You do not need to edit anything yourself.
